outcome: Still open at 11 Oct 2026. Since 26 Jan 2024 there are two new items with mathematical content: a single-author Zenodo preprint (Philippe Cochin, 9 Sep 2026) giving conditional lower bounds on hypothetical nontrivial cycles of the juggler map, with the author's use of large language models disclosed; and a web page (Ulrich Neuenschwander, last updated 12 May 2026) reporting a numerical check that every starting value up to 7110200 reaches 1. Neither settles the statement, and the Cochin record says so itself.
problem_asks: Whether every positive integer n generates a juggler sequence that terminates at 1. Parts: (1) the universal quantifier over all positive integers n; (2) the juggler map a(k+1) = floor(sqrt(a(k))) when a(k) is even and floor(a(k)^(3/2)) when a(k) is odd, started at a(0) = n; (3) the claim that each such trajectory reaches the value 1 after finitely many steps (once at 1 it stays at 1, so terminating at 1 means hitting 1). The statement is a yes/no question with no bound, count or counterexample asked for. A trajectory that never hits 1 either repeats (a cycle, necessarily not through 1) or never repeats; the question covers both ways of failing.

events.what_happened: Pre-window computations of individual juggler trajectories and their peak values by Harry J. Smith, reported in a letter to Clifford Pickover (27 June 1992), including the trajectory from 48443 whose peak term has 972,463 digits and reaches 1 at a157. R. G. Wilson V wrote to N. J. A. Sloane in September 1992 about the same sequence (cited in OEIS A007320). These are trajectory data for particular starting values and do not bear on termination for all n.
events.delivers: Termination and peak data for individual starting values, including 48443. Restricted to the specific trajectories reported; no general claim.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks: no statement about all n.
events.directly_checkable: Individual trajectories can be recomputed with any integer arithmetic; the peak for 48443 is given by Wikipedia and OEIS sources, not recomputed by me.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture: reports trajectories that reach 1. No counterexample.

events.what_happened: The 26 Jan 2024 frozen Wikipedia article states: 'It is conjectured that all juggler sequences eventually reach 1. This conjecture has been verified for initial terms up to 10^6 but has not been proved', citing MathWorld. The latest revision on or before 27 Jan 2024 that I could retrieve is dated 12 Oct 2021, so this wording was in force at the freeze. The origin of the 10^6 check is not traced; the statement is repeated by Rosetta Code and a Medium essay.
events.revisions: Wikipedia wording in force at 2024-01-27 is the 2021-10-12 revision; the 10^6 sentence was replaced on 2026-05-12 (see neuenschwander-2026-05).
events.delivers: A finite verification that all initial terms up to 10^6 reach 1, as stated by the source. Restricted to starting values up to 10^6; no general claim.
events.directly_checkable: Any starting value up to 10^6 can be rechecked by direct iteration; the check itself was not reproduced.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture: no counterexample up to 10^6.

events.what_happened: Theophilus Agama, 'The theory of the Collatz process and the method of dynamical balls', arXiv:1910.13828. The paper is about Collatz. A search snippet (not the full text, which I could not read) says it treats the juggler convergence problem as 'another problem of possibly similar difficulty' and that such problems are 'widely believed to be difficult'. This is a remark, not a result on the juggler map. Version history from the arXiv abstract page: v1 29 Oct 2019, v2 31 Oct 2019, v3 23 Feb 2022, v4 9 Mar 2026.
events.revisions: v4 dated 9 Mar 2026 is the version I saw listed. Earliest version carrying the juggler remark is not established (v1 PDF text was unreadable); the date given is v4's, so the first public mention may be earlier.
events.delivers: Nothing on juggler convergence. It states a view about relative difficulty.
events.direction: None: a remark that the problem is hard, not a result about it.

events.what_happened: Assale Adje, 'On the Maximization of Real Sequences', arXiv:2506.18409 (math.OC, math.DS). A general method for the maximal term of a real sequence, with a truncation index. In the introduction it notes that the 'maximum excursion value' terminology is used for Syracuse sequences and, in its reference [22], for juggler sequences (see [20]); in both cases the value is the maximum of the sequence. The juggler material is a remark in the introduction. The portion of the text I read did not contain a juggler result.
events.revisions: v1 23 Jun 2025; v2 1 Mar 2026 (per arXiv abstract page). Juggler remark seen in the v2 HTML.
events.delivers: A general method for maxima of real sequences. Not a result about juggler sequences as far as I read; juggler sequences are named as an example of the 'maximum excursion value'.
events.direction: None on termination. The paper's reference [22] for juggler sequences is the source that might carry juggler content; I could not read the bibliography.

events.what_happened: A 2025 preprint 'Estimates of the Maximum Excursion Constant and Stopping Constant of Juggler-like Sequences' by V. Prasad and M. A. Prasad. I did not locate or open it. The title, if accurate, concerns growth constants (maximum excursion and stopping time), not termination.
events.delivers: Unknown. Per the title only: estimates of maximum excursion and stopping constants for juggler-like sequences. Not established that it covers the juggler map itself.
events.remains: Unknown; the title does not indicate that termination for all n is addressed.
events.doubts: Existence and content unverified: seen only as citations in an AI-written secondary source and in a reference list I could not read.

events.what_happened: OEIS A094683 (the juggler step map, values a(n) for n up to 10000 in the linked b-file by Karl V. Boddy) records that a(1521), a(8281), a(9025) and a(9801) were corrected by Zhuorui He on 17 Aug 2026. These are corrections to table values, not a trajectory-termination result.
events.delivers: Four corrected table entries for the step map at n up to 10000. Nothing about termination.

events.what_happened: A web page 'Juggler Sequences' at derneueschwan.ch/juggler, 'Last update: 2026-05-12', with a linked Python script juggler.py whose header reads '#Juggler sequence brute force calculator' and '#2026-05-12, Ulrich Neuenschwander'. The page states that the conjecture 'has been numerically verified for x0 values of up to 7110200, using a tailored Python script'; that 'the first value, for which convergence has not been shown yet, is 7110201'; that 'the conjecture has not been proven thus far'; and that 'in this range, xi values reach up to 108000000'. It credits the conjecture to C.A. Pickover. The script uses exact integer square roots (isqrt(temp) for even terms, isqrt(temp**3) for odd terms), caches intermediate values above 10,000 digits in juggler_cache.txt (writes capped at 3 GB), and appends results to juggler_results.txt. The Wikipedia article's verified-range sentence was changed to 7110200 in a revision timestamped 2026-05-12 07:55:54 UTC by user Ueli.n, citing this page.
events.revisions: The page shows only 'Last update: 2026-05-12'. The first posting date is not established: the Wayback capture was refused and I could not find an earlier version. The date given is the last-update date, which is the earliest date I can attribute.
events.delivers: A numerical check, per the page's own claim, that every starting value up to 7110200 reaches 1. This is finitely many instances of the universal claim: it moves the verified range but not the conjecture, which the page itself says is unproven.
events.remains: Every starting value above 7110200 (the page's own first unverified value is 7110201), and so the universal statement in problem_asks.
events.directly_checkable: The script juggler.py is linked from the page and can be rerun by anyone to recompute the range. I did not run it. The page describes it as brute force with cache-based early stopping.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture: reports no starting value up to 7110200 that fails to reach 1. Moves only the verified range.
people: Ulrich Neuenschwander (named in the script header, not on the page)

events.what_happened: Philippe Cochin, 'Lower Bounds for Cycle Lengths in the Juggler Map' (the record's alternative title is 'Cycle financing and period lower bounds for the Juggler map'), Zenodo preprint v1.0.0, CC BY 4.0, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22676453. It restricts hypothetical nontrivial cycles of the juggler map. It proves a 'cycle-financing' inequality relating the minimum n, length L and number of odd steps o of a cycle, and refines it with an irrational rotation, Denjoy-Koksma estimates and Ostrowski decompositions. Combined with verified descent inputs described in the paper, it gives period lower bounds of 25781, 176251, 478245 and 780239 at floors 10^6, 26254995, 162849448 and 350000000. Finite-word exclusions give at least four even steps without a descent-floor input; a computational classification strengthens this to eight even steps and period at least 22. The core inequalities and selected classifications are stated to be formalized in Lean 4. The key inequality as printed on the record: 'nlog n (3^(o) - 2^(L)) <= L 3^(o)'. The record states: 'Neither the exclusion of all nontrivial cycles nor universal termination is established.' OEIS A007320 cites it in its references as 'Philippe Cochin, Lower Bounds for Cycle Lengths in the Juggler Map (2026)' with this DOI.
events.revisions: v1.0.0 published 9 Sep 2026. The record page says a newer version exists; I did not retrieve it (the versions page returned 404), so what changed is unknown.
events.delivers: Within the record's own framing: for any hypothetical nontrivial cycle of the juggler map, lower bounds on its minimum n, length and odd-step count via the cycle-financing inequality, and the period lower bounds at the listed floors. Restricted to cycles; the record does not claim to exclude all nontrivial cycles, and does not claim universal termination. The period bounds rest on 'verified descent inputs described in the paper', which I could not read. The record does not, as far as the page shows, address trajectories that diverge to infinity.
events.remains: The whole statement. The record disclaims both exclusion of all nontrivial cycles and universal termination. The divergence half of 'every trajectory reaches 1' is not addressed in what I read. The bounds are for hypothetical cycles only.
events.directly_checkable: The key inequality is printed on the record page; checking it needs the paper's derivation, which I did not read. Descent computations and per-length comparisons are said to be separate from the Lean proofs; no code was retrieved and no Lean repository was found.
events.doubts: (1) Self-published single-author Zenodo preprint; author listed only as 'Researcher'. I found no affiliation, no journal submission, and no earlier publications by this author in this area. (2) The author discloses heavy LLM use (quoted in ai). The record also says the 'verified descent inputs' and the 'descent-floor' argument are in the paper I could not read, so the period bounds cannot be traced from what I saw. (3) The Lean formalization is said to cover 'core inequalities and selected classifications', not the whole argument; I did not find the repository or whether it contains sorry. (4) A newer version exists and was not retrieved.
events.direction: Toward the conjecture, in part: it bounds what any nontrivial cycle would have to look like and reports none. It does not claim to resolve the conjecture, and the record says so.

summary: Status at 11 Oct 2026: open, and no event found settles the statement. Two items in the window carry mathematical content. (a) Philippe Cochin's single-author Zenodo preprint of 9 Sep 2026, 'Lower Bounds for Cycle Lengths in the Juggler Map', restricts hypothetical nontrivial cycles (a cycle-financing inequality, period lower bounds at four floors, finite-word exclusions up to eight even steps). Its own record says neither exclusion of all nontrivial cycles nor universal termination is established. OEIS A007320 cites it. I found no human engagement with it. The record discloses that the author 'used large language models throughout the development of this work, including ... proposing and developing proof arguments, writing Lean formalizations'. No specific model is named, so ai.systems carries the generic phrase and none_found is false. The disclosure is load-bearing on its face, since the authors say LLMs proposed proof arguments, but the record gives no further account of which arguments. (b) Ulrich Neuenschwander's page at derneueschwan.ch/juggler, 'Last update 2026-05-12', reports a numerical check of all starting values up to 7110200 (first unverified value 7110201) with a Python script. Nothing on the page mentions AI. Wikipedia's article changed its verified bound from 10^6 to 7110200 in a revision timestamped 2026-05-12, citing that page. The frozen January 2024 wording was 10^6. Per §2.1, a finite check moves the verified range, not the universal claim. The first posting date of the page is not established: its Wayback capture was refused. The page's author is inferred from the script header only; the Wikipedia editor 'Ueli.n' may or may not be the same person, which I did not establish. Discounted events: Agama's Collatz paper (v4, 9 Mar 2026) remarks that juggler convergence is of possibly similar difficulty, which I saw only in a search snippet; Adje's arXiv 2506.18409 (June 2025) names juggler sequences only in its introduction; OEIS A094683's b-file had four table entries corrected by Zhuorui He on 17 Aug 2026. Unverified lead: a 2025 Prasad and Prasad preprint on the maximum excursion and stopping constants of juggler-like sequences, cited only by Grokipedia (an AI-written encyclopedia that says it was 'written and fact-checked by Grok') and in a reference list I could not read; I could not locate the preprint. Pre-window: Smith and Wilson's 1992 trajectory computations and the 10^6 check. Searches: 52 WebSearch calls, plus page fetches; AI-specific searches (AlphaEvolve, AlphaProof, OpenAI, GPT-5, Gemini Deep Think, OEIS Open, Erdős database, FrontierMath, Aristotle, Lean/mathlib, 'AI-generated proof claim') found no AI-attributed result on this problem. The OEIS Open benchmark paper (arXiv 2608.11941) does not mention juggler sequences. Close calls: (i) whether Cochin's record is a partial result on this problem: it restricts one of the two ways a trajectory can fail to reach 1 (cycles), not the other (divergence), and it rests on inputs I could not read; (ii) whether a generic LLM disclosure counts as AI involvement in the substantive mathematics: the authors' sentence says LLMs proposed proof arguments, but it names no system and gives no detail.
competing_reading: Cochin's record could be read as the first substantive progress on this problem since the freeze: it constrains every possible nontrivial cycle with explicit period bounds, and its core inequalities are said to be formalized in Lean 4. Against that: the record disclaims both cycle exclusion and universal termination; the period bounds depend on descent inputs in a paper I did not read; the preprint is self-published by an author with no visible background in the area and is LLM-assisted with no named model; and nothing in the record shows that the LLM-proposed proof arguments were checked by a qualified reader. On the AI side, the disclosure is strong ('proposing and developing proof arguments') but names no system, so the AI question for that event rests on the author's sentence alone. The Neuenschwander check could be read as moving the problem's status, but finite verification of the universal claim does not change what the conjecture asserts, and the page itself says it is unproven.
what_would_settle_it: For Cochin: the full paper, in particular the 'verified descent inputs' and the floors 26254995, 162849448 and 350000000; the Lean repository and whether it contains sorry, and whether the period bounds rather than only the inequalities are formalized; the newer version and what changed; a qualified reader's account of the cycle-financing argument; and any argument addressing divergent trajectories. For the AI question: which model or product the author used and for which proof steps. For Neuenschwander: a rerun of juggler.py, the page's first posting date (Wayback capture), and whether the page author is the Wikipedia editor. For the Prasad preprint: the paper itself and whether it treats termination or only growth constants.

events.ai_basis: The author used large language models throughout the development of this work, including drafting and revising the prose, proposing and developing proof arguments, writing Lean formalizations, and designing and implementing computations.

judgement.why: The statement is a yes/no universal claim. Smith's trajectories, the 10^6 check and Neuenschwander's check to 7110200 are finite verifications (instances). Agama and Adje only mention juggler sequences; the OEIS b-file correction concerns step-map values, not termination (none). Prasad is known only by its title, which is about growth constants, a changed question (variant). Agama's date is v4's and the earliest version carrying the remark is unknown, so it is left null. Cochin is the close call. It gives lower bounds on the period of any hypothetical nontrivial cycle, and some of them (at least eight even steps, period at least 22) are unconditional. That moves a quantity on a question that stays open, so it is bound rather than none or case, because it excludes no class of n and does not address divergence. It is unreviewed and doubtful. Its AI disclosure says LLMs were 'proposing and developing proof arguments', which is mathematics in the result. The work is presented as the author's own, so the role is assisted rather than generated.
judgement.doubts: Cochin's AI role rests on a generic disclosure with no named model and no account of which arguments came from the LLM; it might arguably be generated. Its scope could also be read as none if the period bounds are judged to be mainly products of finite descent verification.
